gives weights $1,4,2,\ldots,4,1$. The even condition
$n\ge2$ makes the number of blocks a positive integer. The formula is an exact-real

Let $Q:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ be a finite quadrature functional of the form
$$Q(g)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i g(x_i),$$
where $m\ge1$, the nodes $x_i\in[0,1]$ are distinct, and $w_i\in\mathbb R$.
A one-dimensional **nested level hierarchy** is a sequence
$(Q_\ell)_{\ell\in\mathbb N_0}$ of such functionals, with node sets
$X_\ell=\{x_{\ell,i}:1\le i\le m_\ell\}$ satisfying
$X_{\ell-1}\subseteq X_\ell$ for every $\ell\ge1$.
Set $Q_{-1}:=0$, the zero functional, and define the **detail functional**
$$\Delta_0:=Q_0,\qquad \Delta_\ell:=Q_\ell-Q_{\ell-1}\quad(\ell\ge1).$$
Finite sums are as in [[def-finite-sum]]. For each $d\ge1$, the integration
functional used below is $I_d(f):=\int_{[0,1]^d}f$, with the multiple Riemann
integral convention of [[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]].

The convergence and rate results in this pair use the **dyadic composite-
Simpson hierarchy**
$$Q_\ell(g):=Q_S(g;0,1,2^{\ell+1}),\qquad X_\ell=\{k/2^{\ell+1}:0\le k\le2^{\ell+1}\},$$
where $Q_S$ is the even-panel rule of [[alg-composite-simpson-rule]]. The
number of panels is even and at least two. The sets are nested because
$k/2^{\ell}=2k/2^{\ell+1}$, and their weights are nonnegative with total
weight one: each two-panel block has nonnegative weights $H(1,4,1)/6$
summing to its length $H$, and the blocks partition an interval of length one.
Level zero has nodes $0,1/2,1$ and weights $1/6,4/6,1/6$.

For a multi-index $\ell=(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d$, any tensor
product $R_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes R_{\ell_d}^{(d)}$ of these
finite functionals means the finite weighted functional obtained by multiplying
the coordinate weights and evaluating on the corresponding node tuples. In
particular, $\Delta_\ell:=\Delta_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes
\Delta_{\ell_d}^{(d)}$. No exactness or error property is implied by the
notation alone.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

A bounded $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ on a nondegenerate rectangle is Riemann
integrable if and only if, for every $\varepsilon>0$, some grid $P$ satisfies
$U(f,P)-L(f,P)<\varepsilon$.

A **grid partition** $P$ of a nondegenerate rectangle $Q=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is a family, one for each $j<m$, of one-dimensional partitions $a_j=t_{j,0}<\cdots<t_{j,n_j}=b_j$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]). For a multi-index $i=(i_0,\ldots,i_{m-1})$ with $i_j<n_j$, its cell is
$$Q_i:=\prod_{j<m}[t_{j,i_j},t_{j,i_j+1}].$$
A sum over cells means the iterated recursive sum $\sum_{i_0<n_0}\cdots\sum_{i_{m-1}<n_{m-1}}$ of [[def-finite-sum]]. The **mesh** is $\max_{j<m,i_j<n_j}(t_{j,i_j+1}-t_{j,i_j})$, which exists by [[lem-finite-set-has-max]] and is the largest $d_\infty$-diameter ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]], [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]).

Refinement is coordinatewise. Coordinatewise union gives a common refinement. The cells cover $Q$ and have pairwise disjoint interiors. Repeated splitting of finite sums and induction on $m$ give
$$\sum_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i)=\operatorname{vol}(Q).$$
These statements include boundary overlaps: boundaries may meet, but interiors do not, and volume splitting is algebraic.

Let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be bounded on a nondegenerate rectangle and let $P$ be a grid. For each cell $Q_i$, put
$$m_i:=\inf f[Q_i],\quad M_i:=\sup f[Q_i],\quad L(f,P):=\sum_i m_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i),\quad U(f,P):=\sum_i M_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i).$$
The extrema exist as finite reals because each nonempty image is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]), and the sums use the iterated convention of [[def-multidimensional-grid-partition]].

Since $m_i\le M_i$ and cell volumes are nonnegative, $L(f,P)\le U(f,P)$. Moreover
$$U(f,P)-L(f,P)=\sum_i(M_i-m_i)\operatorname{vol}(Q_i),$$
the sum of cell oscillations weighted by volume ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

For a bounded function $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ on a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, define
$$\underline{\int_Q}f:=\sup_P L(f,P),\qquad \overline{\int_Q}f:=\inf_P U(f,P),$$
over all grid partitions $P$ of $Q$. The grid family is nonempty, since the endpoints in each coordinate give a one-cell grid. Every lower sum is at most every upper sum by a common refinement and [[lem-multidimensional-refinement-inequalities]], so the two sets of sums are nonempty and bounded and the extrema exist ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]).

The function is **Riemann integrable over $Q$** when the two values agree.
Their unique common real is $\int_Q f$. No integral is defined here for a
degenerate rectangle, because the grid definition requires every coordinate
interval to have distinct endpoints. This is the multidimensional Darboux
definition; its agreement with the published one-dimensional definition is
proved separately.

The sum is a finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Each two-panel block

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]).

1. If $|r| < 1$ then $(r^k)$ is **null**, that is $r^k \to 0$
   ([[def-real-limit]]).
2. If $|r| > 1$ then $(|r|^k)$ **diverges to $+\infty$**
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]).

Claim 2 is stated for $|r|^k$ and not for $r^k$ on purpose: for $r < -1$ the
terms $r^k$ alternate in sign and are unbounded, so they neither converge nor
diverge to $+\infty$; what is true of them is the statement about their absolute
values.

Both claims come from Bernoulli's inequality ([[lem-bernoulli-inequality]]) and
the Archimedean property. Nothing here needs the least-upper-bound property
except through [[thm-of-archimedean]] and [[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]].

A sequence $(x_k)$ of reals **converges** to $x \in \mathbb{R}$ when for
every rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $K$ with
$|x_k - x| < \hat\varepsilon$ for all $k \ge K$. It is **Cauchy** when for
every rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $K$ with
$|x_k - x_l| < \hat\varepsilon$ for all $k, l \ge K$.

Let $a, b$ be elements of a field ([[def-field]]) and let integer powers be as in
[[def-integer-power]].

1. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$: $a^{m+n} = a^m a^n$, $(a^m)^n = a^{mn}$ and $(ab)^n = a^n b^n$.
2. If $a \ne 0$ then $a^n \ne 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and $a^{-m} = (a^m)^{-1}$ for every $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ ([[def-int-operations]]).
3. If $a \ne 0$ and $b \ne 0$ then all three identities of claim 1 hold for all $m, n \in \mathbb{Z}$.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

Let $F$ be an ordered field, with field structure as in [[def-field]], and for
$n \ge 1$ let $n \cdot 1_F$ denote the canonical natural number
$\underbrace{1_F + \cdots + 1_F}_{n}$, defined recursively by $1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F$
and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F + 1_F$. Then for every $n \ge 1$:

- $n \cdot 1_F > 0$ and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F > n \cdot 1_F$;
- the map $n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F$ is strictly increasing, hence injective, on $\{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$;
- $(m+n) \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + n \cdot 1_F$ and $(mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F)$ for all $m, n \ge 1$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ then $a^{-1} > 0$.
2. If $0 < a < b$ then $0 < b^{-1} < a^{-1}$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b, c \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ and $b > 0$ then $ab > 0$.
2. If $a > 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab < 0$.
3. If $a < 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab > 0$.
4. If $c > 0$ then $a < b \iff ac < bc$.
5. If $c < 0$ then $a < b \iff bc < ac$ (multiplication by a negative reverses order).

derivations.claim: Fix $\varepsilon>0$. By [F2] and [F3], $f$ is uniformly continuous on $[0,1]^d$. Choose $\delta>0$ such that $\|x-y\|_2<\delta$ implies $|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon$. By [F12], $\delta/\sqrt d>0$; use [F11] to choose a positive rational $\rho<\delta/\sqrt d$, then [F10] to choose $L$ with $H=2^{-L}<\rho$. Thus $\sqrt d\,H<\delta$, and every cell of the uniform $d$-dimensional grid has diameter $\sqrt d\,H$.

For the $L$ chosen in step 1.1, the tensor Simpson rule is the sum over grid cells of their tensor two-panel block rules: each cell contributes $H^d$ times a weighted average of its $3^d$ endpoint/midpoint tensor nodes, with coefficients $\prod_{j=1}^d(1,4,1)_{i_j}/6^d$. These coefficients are nonnegative and sum to one by [F7]. Each closed cell is compact and nonempty, so [F9] gives finite infimum and supremum of $f$ there. Every node lies in its cell and its value lies between those extrema. Regrouping finite sums by [F8] gives $L(f,P_L)\le Q_L^{\otimes d}(f)\le U(f,P_L)$, with the factors $H^d$ equal to cell volumes.

By step 1.1, the oscillation of $f$ on each cell is at most $\varepsilon$. Thus [F5]–[F6] give $U(f,P_L)-L(f,P_L)\le\varepsilon\sum_C\operatorname{vol}(C)=\varepsilon$. By [F4], $I_d(f)$ lies between these Darboux sums; step 2.1 places the tensor-Simpson value between them as well. Therefore $|Q_L^{\otimes d}(f)-I_d(f)|\le\varepsilon$. This holds for sufficiently large $L$ for each $\varepsilon>0$, proving convergence.

invalid-Simpson-panel-count. If $n$ is even, put
$h=(b-a)/n$ and $x_j=a+jh$ for $0\le j\le n$; return

$$Q_S(f;a,b,n):=\frac h3\sum_{j<n/2}\bigl(f(x_{2j})+4f(x_{2j+1})+f(x_{2j+2})\bigr).$$

The sum is a finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Each two-panel block
$[x_{2j},x_{2j+2}]$ uses its endpoints and midpoint. Expanding the block sum
gives weights $1,4,2,\ldots,4,1$. The even condition
$n\ge2$ makes the number of blocks a positive integer. The formula is an exact-real
procedure; floating point evaluation and summation error are separate from

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and $f:I\to\mathbb R$. Put $f^{(0)}:=f$. Recursively, wherever $f^{(j)}$ is differentiable, put $f^{(j+1)}:=(f^{(j)})'$, with derivatives at endpoints understood in the one-sided sense fixed by [[def-derivative]] and [[def-one-sided-limits]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, the function is **$k$-times differentiable** on $I$ if $f^{(j)}$ exists on $I$ for every $j\le k$. It is of class **$C^k$** on $I$ if these derivatives exist and every $f^{(j)}$, $0\le j\le k$, is continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). It is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, if it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]] and the absolute value as in

$$\Big|\sum_{k<n} a_k\Big| \le \sum_{k<n} |a_k|.$$

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).

5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Let $a, b$ be elements of a field ([[def-field]]) and let integer powers be as in
[[def-integer-power]].

1. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$: $a^{m+n} = a^m a^n$, $(a^m)^n = a^{mn}$ and $(ab)^n = a^n b^n$.
2. If $a \ne 0$ then $a^n \ne 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and $a^{-m} = (a^m)^{-1}$ for every $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ ([[def-int-operations]]).
3. If $a \ne 0$ and $b \ne 0$ then all three identities of claim 1 hold for all $m, n \in \mathbb{Z}$.

Let $Q:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ be a finite quadrature functional of the form
$$Q(g)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i g(x_i),$$
where $m\ge1$, the nodes $x_i\in[0,1]$ are distinct, and $w_i\in\mathbb R$.
A one-dimensional **nested level hierarchy** is a sequence
$(Q_\ell)_{\ell\in\mathbb N_0}$ of such functionals, with node sets
$X_\ell=\{x_{\ell,i}:1\le i\le m_\ell\}$ satisfying
$X_{\ell-1}\subseteq X_\ell$ for every $\ell\ge1$.
Set $Q_{-1}:=0$, the zero functional, and define the **detail functional**
$$\Delta_0:=Q_0,\qquad \Delta_\ell:=Q_\ell-Q_{\ell-1}\quad(\ell\ge1).$$
Finite sums are as in [[def-finite-sum]]. For each $d\ge1$, the integration
functional used below is $I_d(f):=\int_{[0,1]^d}f$, with the multiple Riemann
integral convention of [[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]].

The convergence and rate results in this pair use the **dyadic composite-
Simpson hierarchy**
$$Q_\ell(g):=Q_S(g;0,1,2^{\ell+1}),\qquad X_\ell=\{k/2^{\ell+1}:0\le k\le2^{\ell+1}\},$$
where $Q_S$ is the even-panel rule of [[alg-composite-simpson-rule]]. The
number of panels is even and at least two. The sets are nested because
$k/2^{\ell}=2k/2^{\ell+1}$, and their weights are nonnegative with total
weight one: each two-panel block has nonnegative weights $H(1,4,1)/6$
summing to its length $H$, and the blocks partition an interval of length one.
Level zero has nodes $0,1/2,1$ and weights $1/6,4/6,1/6$.

For a multi-index $\ell=(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d$, any tensor
product $R_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes R_{\ell_d}^{(d)}$ of these
finite functionals means the finite weighted functional obtained by multiplying
the coordinate weights and evaluating on the corresponding node tuples. In
particular, $\Delta_\ell:=\Delta_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes
\Delta_{\ell_d}^{(d)}$. No exactness or error property is implied by the
notation alone.

Fix a dimension $d\ge1$. A finite set $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb N_0^d$ is
**downward closed** if, whenever $\ell\in\Lambda$ and $\ell_j>0$, the index
$\ell-e_j$ also belongs to $\Lambda$; here $e_j$ is the $j$th coordinate unit
vector. In this pair an admissible Smolyak set is a nonempty finite downward-
closed $\Lambda$ that contains $0$.

For a level hierarchy from [[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]], define
the **Smolyak cubature functional**
$$Q_\Lambda(f):=\sum_{\ell\in\Lambda}(\Delta_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes\Delta_{\ell_d}^{(d)})(f).$$
Each summand is a finite signed weighted sum. Expanding all differences and
adding coefficients at equal points gives one finite signed weight for each
distinct node in
$$\mathcal N_\Lambda:=\bigcup_{\ell\in\Lambda}X_{\ell_1}\times\cdots\times X_{\ell_d}.$$
The **node-union work count** for this direct evaluation convention is
$W(\Lambda):=|\mathcal N_\Lambda|$, so shared nodes are counted once. A
combined weight may be negative or zero; no positivity claim follows from the
definition.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Let $(M,\cdot,e)$ be a monoid ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]) and let
$g : \mathbb{N} \to M$ be a family of elements of $M$, written $g_i := g(i)$.
There is exactly one function $P_g : \mathbb{N} \to M$ satisfying

$$P_g(0) = e, \qquad P_g(\sigma(n)) = P_g(n) \cdot g_n \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}),$$

and we write

$$\prod_{i<n} g_i \;:=\; P_g(n), \qquad \text{also written } g_0 g_1 \cdots g_{n-1}.$$

In particular the **empty product** is $\prod_{i<0} g_i = e$, and
$\prod_{i<1} g_i = e \cdot g_0 = g_0$.

**Why the recursion is legitimate.** The clause $P_g(\sigma(n)) = P_g(n) \cdot g_n$
consults $n$ as well as $P_g(n)$, so [[thm-recursion]] does not apply to it
directly. Apply that theorem instead with the set $A = \mathbb{N} \times M$, the
element $a = (0,e)$, and the function $F : A \to A$ given by
$F(n,x) = (\sigma(n),\, x \cdot g_n)$: it yields a unique
$H : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times M$ with $H(0) = (0,e)$ and
$H(\sigma(n)) = F(H(n))$. Writing $H(n) = (H_1(n), H_2(n))$, induction
([[thm-induction-principle]]) gives $H_1(n) = n$ for every $n$, since $H_1(0) = 0$
and $H_1(\sigma(n)) = \sigma(H_1(n))$. Hence
$H(\sigma(n)) = (\sigma(n),\, H_2(n) \cdot g_n)$, so $P_g := H_2$ satisfies the two
displayed equations. It is the only such function: if $Q$ satisfies them too, then
$\{ n : P_g(n) = Q(n) \}$ contains $0$ and is closed under $\sigma$, hence is all
of $\mathbb{N}$ by induction.

**The value depends only on $g_0,\dots,g_{n-1}$.** If $g, g' : \mathbb{N} \to M$
satisfy $g_i = g'_i$ for every $i < n$, then $P_g(n) = P_{g'}(n)$. Indeed the set
of $n$ for which this implication holds contains $0$, both products then being
$e$; and if it holds at $n$, and $g, g'$ agree at every $i < \sigma(n)$, then they
agree at every $i < n$ and also at $n$ itself, because $i < \sigma(n)$ is
equivalent to $i \le n$ ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so
$P_g(\sigma(n)) = P_g(n) \cdot g_n = P_{g'}(n) \cdot g'_n = P_{g'}(\sigma(n))$.
Induction finishes it. This is what makes the notation $g_0 g_1 \cdots g_{n-1}$
unambiguous: it names a value determined by the first $n$ terms alone, and a
finite list $u$ of length $n$, that is a function $u : n \to M$ on the von Neumann
natural $n = \{0,\dots,n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), determines the product
$\prod_{i<n} u_i := P_{\tilde u}(n)$ computed from any extension
$\tilde u : \mathbb{N} \to M$ of $u$.

derivations.claim: Fix any one-dimensional input $g$ and coordinate $j$, and put $c_r:=Q_r(g)$. By [F3], $\sum_{r=1}^{m_j}(c_r-c_{r-1})=c_{m_j}-c_0$; for $m_j=0$ this is the empty-sum identity. Adding $Q_0(g)$ and using [F1] yields $\sum_{r=0}^{m_j}\Delta_r(g)=Q_{m_j}(g)$. Since $g$ was arbitrary, this is equality of functionals.

Expand $\bigotimes_{j=1}^d\left(\sum_{r=0}^{m_j}\Delta_r^{(j)}\right)$ by distributing each finite coordinate sum. By [F3]–[F4] the resulting terms are exactly the tensor details indexed once by $R_m$, which is the Smolyak sum $Q_{R_m}$ by [F2]. Applying step 1.1 in every coordinate identifies this expansion with $Q_{m_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes Q_{m_d}^{(d)}$, as claimed.

Let $Q:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ be a finite quadrature functional of the form
$$Q(g)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i g(x_i),$$
where $m\ge1$, the nodes $x_i\in[0,1]$ are distinct, and $w_i\in\mathbb R$.
A one-dimensional **nested level hierarchy** is a sequence
$(Q_\ell)_{\ell\in\mathbb N_0}$ of such functionals, with node sets
$X_\ell=\{x_{\ell,i}:1\le i\le m_\ell\}$ satisfying
$X_{\ell-1}\subseteq X_\ell$ for every $\ell\ge1$.
Set $Q_{-1}:=0$, the zero functional, and define the **detail functional**
$$\Delta_0:=Q_0,\qquad \Delta_\ell:=Q_\ell-Q_{\ell-1}\quad(\ell\ge1).$$
Finite sums are as in [[def-finite-sum]]. For each $d\ge1$, the integration
functional used below is $I_d(f):=\int_{[0,1]^d}f$, with the multiple Riemann
integral convention of [[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]].

The convergence and rate results in this pair use the **dyadic composite-
Simpson hierarchy**
$$Q_\ell(g):=Q_S(g;0,1,2^{\ell+1}),\qquad X_\ell=\{k/2^{\ell+1}:0\le k\le2^{\ell+1}\},$$
where $Q_S$ is the even-panel rule of [[alg-composite-simpson-rule]]. The
number of panels is even and at least two. The sets are nested because
$k/2^{\ell}=2k/2^{\ell+1}$, and their weights are nonnegative with total
weight one: each two-panel block has nonnegative weights $H(1,4,1)/6$
summing to its length $H$, and the blocks partition an interval of length one.
Level zero has nodes $0,1/2,1$ and weights $1/6,4/6,1/6$.

For a multi-index $\ell=(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d$, any tensor
product $R_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes R_{\ell_d}^{(d)}$ of these
finite functionals means the finite weighted functional obtained by multiplying
the coordinate weights and evaluating on the corresponding node tuples. In
particular, $\Delta_\ell:=\Delta_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes
\Delta_{\ell_d}^{(d)}$. No exactness or error property is implied by the
notation alone.

Fix a dimension $d\ge1$. A finite set $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb N_0^d$ is
**downward closed** if, whenever $\ell\in\Lambda$ and $\ell_j>0$, the index
$\ell-e_j$ also belongs to $\Lambda$; here $e_j$ is the $j$th coordinate unit
vector. In this pair an admissible Smolyak set is a nonempty finite downward-
closed $\Lambda$ that contains $0$.

For a level hierarchy from [[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]], define
the **Smolyak cubature functional**
$$Q_\Lambda(f):=\sum_{\ell\in\Lambda}(\Delta_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes\Delta_{\ell_d}^{(d)})(f).$$
Each summand is a finite signed weighted sum. Expanding all differences and
adding coefficients at equal points gives one finite signed weight for each
distinct node in
$$\mathcal N_\Lambda:=\bigcup_{\ell\in\Lambda}X_{\ell_1}\times\cdots\times X_{\ell_d}.$$
The **node-union work count** for this direct evaluation convention is
$W(\Lambda):=|\mathcal N_\Lambda|$, so shared nodes are counted once. A
combined weight may be negative or zero; no positivity claim follows from the
definition.

Let $d\ge1$ and $m=(m_1,\ldots,m_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d$. For
$R_m:=\{\ell\in\mathbb N_0^d:0\le\ell_j\le m_j\text{ for every }j\}$ and
the details of [[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]],
$$\sum_{\ell\in R_m}\Delta_\ell=Q_{m_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes Q_{m_d}^{(d)}.$$

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles. If $a:A\to\mathbb R$ and $b:B\to\mathbb R$ are continuous and $f(x,y):=a(x)b(y)$, then
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\left(\int_Aa\right)\left(\int_Bb\right).$$
In particular, if $f(x,y)=a(x)$ is independent of $y$, then $\int_{A\times B}f=\operatorname{vol}(B)\int_Aa$.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Let $a<b$, let $n\ge2$ be an even integer, and let
$p(x)=c_0+c_1x+c_2x^2+c_3x^3$ with real coefficients. Then

$$\int_a^b p(x)\,dx=Q_S(p;a,b,n),$$

where $Q_S$ is the composite Simpson value of
[[alg-composite-simpson-rule]].

derivations.claim: Fix a tensor polynomial $p(x)=\prod_{j=1}^dp_j(x_j)$. If some $\ell_j>q_j$, then $\ell_j-1\ge q_j$, so [A1] makes both $Q_{\ell_j}$ and $Q_{\ell_j-1}$ exact on $p_j$; hence $\Delta_{\ell_j}(p_j)=0$. Therefore every tensor detail with $\ell\notin R_q$ vanishes on $p$.

Since $R_q\subseteq\Lambda$, [F2] and step 1.1 reduce $Q_\Lambda(p)$ to the rectangular detail sum. By [F3] this is $\prod_{j=1}^d Q_{q_j}(p_j)$, which equals $\prod_j\int_0^1p_j$ by [A1]. Repeated application of [F4] identifies this product with $I_d(p)$.

Every stated tensor polynomial is a finite linear combination of products handled in step 2.1. The finite rule and the multiple integral are linear by [F5]–[F6], so exactness extends term by term. If $\sum_jq_j\le n$, every $\ell\in R_q$ has $|\ell|_1\le n$, hence $R_q\subseteq\Lambda_n$, proving the isotropic-simplex claim.

For the hierarchy of [[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]], each level has panel count $2^{\ell+1}$, which is even and at least two. Thus [F7] makes every $Q_\ell$ exact through degree three. Set $r_\ell=3$ for all $\ell$; for coordinate degrees $s_j\le3$ the least levels are $q_j=0$, so $R_q=\{0\}\subseteq\Lambda$. Step 3.1 gives the stated exactness for these tensor polynomials.

**Input:** dimension $d\ge1$; a finite downward-closed cap
$\Gamma\subseteq\mathbb N_0^d$ containing $0$; for each coordinate, the
one-dimensional quadrature rules from a hierarchy as in
[[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]] through every level used by
$\Gamma$, with canonical node keys that agree exactly if and only if the real
nodes agree and are totally ordered; a function $f$ evaluable at the nodes; and
an integer evaluation budget $B\ge0$. Admissible inputs supply all these rules
and keys at every level required by $\Gamma$.

**Output:** a current downward-closed index set $\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma$, its
Smolyak value when the initial rule fits the budget, the computed detail
surpluses, the distinct nodes actually sampled, and one status:
`budget-too-small`, `budget-exhausted`, or `frontier-exhausted`.

1. An index $\ell\in\Gamma\setminus\Lambda$ is **admissible** when every
   immediate predecessor $\ell-e_j$ with $\ell_j>0$ already belongs to
   $\Lambda$. Its **surplus** is the exact detail value $\delta_\ell(f)$ and
   its selection indicator is $|\delta_\ell(f)|$.
2. Form the baseline node set $X_0^d$. If its cardinality exceeds $B$, return
   `budget-too-small`, an empty $\Lambda$, no cubature value, and no sampled
   nodes. Otherwise set $\Lambda:=\{0\}$, initialize the active candidate set
   as empty, evaluate $f$ once at every baseline node, and set the current
   value to $Q_{\{0\}}(f)$. Then process every initially admissible index in
   $\Gamma\setminus\Lambda$ in lexicographic order using step 3.
3. Visit newly admissible indices in lexicographic order, skipping any index
   already recorded as active, accepted, or `uncomputed-budget`. To compute one
   surplus, form its finite tensor-detail node set and the new keys not already
   sampled. If adding them would exceed $B$, record this candidate as
   `uncomputed-budget` without evaluating those nodes. Otherwise evaluate each
   new key once, store the values, compute $\delta_\ell(f)$ from the finite
   signed weights, and add the index to the active candidate set.
4. If the active set is empty and an admissible `uncomputed-budget` candidate
   remains, return `budget-exhausted`. Otherwise, if the active set is empty,
   return `frontier-exhausted`.
5. Otherwise select the active index with largest absolute surplus, breaking
   ties lexicographically. Remove it from the active set, mark it accepted, add
   it to $\Lambda$, update the cubature value by adding its signed surplus, and
   inspect its finite forward neighbors for newly admissible indices; process
   them by step 3. Repeat from step 4.

The evaluation budget counts the union of distinct keys sampled while computing
both accepted and candidate surpluses. The indicator $|\delta_\ell(f)|$ is a
refinement heuristic only. A threshold on this indicator, or exhaustion of the
finite candidate cap, is not an error certificate unless a separate omitted-tail
bound applies.

N_0^d$ containing $0$, the finitely many levels required by $\Lambda$, a
function $f$ evaluable at their nodes, and for each exact node a canonical key
in a totally ordered set. Keys must agree exactly if and only if the real node
tuples agree. If any required rule or key is missing, return `invalid-input`.

   [[def-smolyak-cubature]] by replacing each coordinate factor
   $\Delta_0$ with $Q_0$ and each $\Delta_r$ ($r\ge1$) with

   lexicographic multi-index order.

   the exact tuple key; initialize an unseen key with coefficient $0$.

   X_{\ell_1}\times\cdots\times X_{\ell_d}$, sort its distinct exact keys, and

comparisons, arithmetic, and function-evaluation error are outside its claims.

Moreover, for every finite $F\subseteq\mathbb N_0^d$,

Let $d\ge1$ and let $f:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. For the dyadic
composite-Simpson hierarchy of [[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]],
the tensor product $Q_L^{\otimes d}$ converges to the multiple Riemann
integral:
$$\lim_{L\to\infty} Q_L^{\otimes d}(f)=I_d(f).$$

Let $d\ge1$, let $f:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, and use a level
hierarchy as in [[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]]. Suppose its tensor
rules satisfy $Q_L^{\otimes d}(f)\to I_d(f)$ and its detail family is absolutely
summable in the sense of [[def-smolyak-absolute-detail-summability]]. For every
finite downward-closed $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb N_0^d$ containing $0$,
$$|I_d(f)-Q_\Lambda(f)|\le\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb N_0^d\setminus\Lambda}|\delta_\ell(f)|.$$
In particular, the dyadic composite-Simpson hierarchy satisfies the convergence
hypothesis for continuous $f$ by
[[lem-smolyak-dyadic-tensor-simpson-convergence]], and for the mixed-derivative
class of [[lem-smolyak-mixed-simpson-detail-decay]] the same hierarchy also
satisfies absolute summability.

Let $m \ge 1$ and write $m = \sigma(M)$, so $M = m-1$. Then for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$

$$\big\lvert\mathcal{W}(n,m)\big\rvert = \binom{n+m-1}{\,m-1\,} = \binom{n+M}{M},$$

and the map
$k \mapsto \big\{\, \big(\sum_{j<\sigma(i)} k_j\big) + i \ :\ i < M \,\big\}$
is a bijection of $\mathcal{W}(n,m)$ onto the set of $M$-element subsets of
$n+M$.

Moreover, for $m \ge 1$ **and $n \ge 1$**,

$$\big\lvert\mathcal{C}(n,m)\big\rvert = \binom{n-1}{\,m-1\,}.$$

**The hypothesis $m \ge 1$ is not decoration.** At $m = 0$ the expression
$\binom{n+m-1}{m-1}$ would require the value $m-1$ at $m = 0$, and
[[def-composition-of-a-natural-number]] records the true counts there:
$\lvert\mathcal{W}(0,0)\rvert = 1$ and $\lvert\mathcal{W}(n,0)\rvert = 0$ for
$n \ge 1$. The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ in the second display is equally load
bearing: at $n = 0$, $m = 1$ the formula would give $\binom{0}{0} = 1$ while
$\mathcal{C}(0,1) = \varnothing$.

Let $n,k \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and $k \ge 1$. Then the number of
compositions of $n$ into exactly $k$ positive parts is

$$\binom{n-1}{k-1}.$$

When $k>n$, there are no such compositions.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), in particular an ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]]) and a field ([[def-field]]), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers ([[def-natural-numbers]]) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
([[def-nat-addition]]).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** ([[thm-induction-principle]]). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
[[thm-recursion]], so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, let $d$ be the
unique natural number satisfying $m+d=n+1$. Existence is the definition of
natural order ([[def-nat-order]]); if $m+d=m+e$, commutativity
([[lem-nat-add-commutative]]) gives $d+m=e+m$, so cancellation
([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]) gives $d=e$. On these admissible bounds only,
we may write this unique additive gap as $d=n+1-m$; no total natural subtraction
operation is presupposed. With $d$ thus fixed, define

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Equivalently, for naturals $m \le r$, the half-open endpoint notation
$\sum_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ and $\prod_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ means
$\sum_{j<d}a_{m+j}$ and $\prod_{j<d}a_{m+j}$, respectively, where $d$ is the
unique natural with $m+d=r$. Here $r-1$ is an endpoint label for the terms
before $r$, so this notation needs no total subtraction operation. For $m=r$,
the unique gap is $0$ because $m+0=m$, giving the empty sum and product; the
case $m=r=0$ is the $-1$ endpoint convention just stipulated.

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in [[def-finite-sum]]. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

For a finite set $A$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$ put

$$[A]^{k} := \{\, S \subseteq A \ :\ \lvert S\rvert = k \,\},$$

the set of $k$-element subsets of $A$. Every $S \subseteq A$ is finite
([[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]]), so the condition $\lvert S\rvert = k$ makes
sense for every subset.

**$[A]^{k}$ is finite.** It is a subset of $\mathcal{P}(A)$, which is finite by
[[cor-cardinality-of-the-power-set]], so [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]] applies.

**$\lvert [A]^{k}\rvert$ depends only on $\lvert A\rvert$.** Let $h : A \to A'$ be
a bijection of finite sets. The direct image map $S \mapsto h[S]$ carries
$[A]^{k}$ into $[A']^{k}$, because $h$ restricted to $S$ is a bijection of $S$
onto $h[S]$ and so $\lvert h[S]\rvert = \lvert S\rvert = k$ by the transport
clause of [[def-finite-cardinality]]; the map $T \mapsto h^{-1}[T]$ is its
two-sided inverse, since $h^{-1}[h[S]] = S$ and $h[h^{-1}[T]] = T$ for a
bijection $h$. So $[A]^{k} \approx [A']^{k}$ and the two have the same
cardinality.

**Definition.** For $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$ set

$$\binom{n}{k} := \big\lvert\, [n]^{k} \,\big\rvert \in \mathbb{N},$$

the **binomial coefficient**. By the previous paragraph and $\lvert n\rvert = n$,

$$\big\lvert [A]^{k}\big\rvert = \binom{\lvert A\rvert}{k} \qquad \text{for every finite } A .$$

**$\binom{n}{k}$ is a count, so it is a natural number by construction.** It is
*not* defined as $n!/(k!\,(n-k)!)$: that expression involves a division, hence
lives in $\mathbb{R}$, and the assertion that its value is a natural number is a
theorem, proved in [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]]. Defining the coefficient as a
count makes integrality free and leaves the closed formula something to prove.

**Boundary values, read off the definition and not stipulated.**

- $\binom{n}{0} = 1$ **for every $n$, including $n = 0$**: the subsets of $n$ of
  cardinality $0$ are exactly the subsets equal to $\varnothing$
  ([[def-finite-cardinality]], clause (b)), so $[n]^{0} = \{\varnothing\}$, a
  one-element set. No empty-product convention is involved.
- $\binom{n}{n} = 1$: if $S \subseteq n$ has $\lvert S\rvert = n = \lvert n\rvert$
  then $S = n$ by clause 3 of [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], so
  $[n]^{n} = \{n\}$.
- $\binom{n}{k} = 0$ for $k > n$: a subset $S \subseteq n$ has
  $\lvert S\rvert \le n$ by clause 2 of [[thm-subset-of-a-finite-set]], so
  $\lvert S\rvert = k > n$ is impossible and $[n]^{k} = \varnothing$
  ([[lem-nat-trichotomy]]).
- $\binom{n}{1} = n$: a subset of cardinality $1$ is $\{x\}$ for exactly one
  $x \in n$, since $\lvert S\rvert = 1$ means $S \approx \{0\}$; so
  $S \mapsto$ its unique element is a bijection $[n]^{1} \to n$.
- $\binom{0}{0} = 1$ and $\binom{0}{k} = 0$ for $k \ge 1$, both instances of the
  above.

For all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$,

$$(x+y)^{n} \;=\; \sum_{k<n+1} \iota\binom{n}{k}\, x^{k}\, y^{\,n-k},$$

where the powers are the integer powers of [[def-integer-power]], the sum is the
real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] over $k = 0, 1, \dots, n$, the difference
$n-k$ is a genuine one because $k \le n$ throughout the range, and $\iota$ is the
canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]].

**The coefficient is $\iota\binom{n}{k}$ and not $\binom{n}{k}$.** A binomial
coefficient is a natural number, that is a von Neumann natural, that is a set; it
is not an element of $\mathbb{R}$, and it enters the field through $\iota$.

**The identity is stated in $\mathbb{R}$ and only in $\mathbb{R}$.** The same
proof uses nothing but commutativity, associativity, distributivity and
natural-number multiples of a ring element, so a commutative-ring version is
available wherever rings are; rings are not available at this point in the
reading order, and the ring statement is a separate statement, to be made where
they are. See the Remarks below.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and $S \subseteq F$.

- $u \in F$ is an **upper bound** of $S$ if $s \le u$ for all $s \in S$; $S$ is
  **bounded above** if it has an upper bound.
- $u \in F$ is a **least upper bound** (or **supremum**, $\sup S$) of $S$ if $u$
  is an upper bound of $S$ and $u \le u'$ for every upper bound $u'$ of $S$.

$F$ is a **complete ordered field** (equivalently, $F$ has the
**least-upper-bound property**, or is **Dedekind complete**) if every nonempty
$S \subseteq F$ that is bounded above has a least upper bound in $F$.

Let $\mathbb{R}$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]), let
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, with powers as in
[[def-integer-power]].

1. **Signs.** If $a \ge 0$ then $a^n \ge 0$, and if $a > 0$ then $a^n > 0$.
2. **Strict monotonicity in the base.** If $0 \le a < b$ and $n \ge 1$ then $a^n < b^n$. Consequently, for $a, b \ge 0$ and $n \ge 1$: $a < b \iff a^n < b^n$ and $a \le b \iff a^n \le b^n$, and $x \mapsto x^n$ is injective on $\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ge 0\}$.
3. **Comparison with the base.** If $a \ge 1$ and $n \ge 1$ then $a^n \ge a \ge 1$; if $a > 1$ and $n \ge 1$ then $a^n \ge a > 1$; and if $0 \le a \le 1$ then $a^n \le 1$.
4. **Monotonicity in the exponent.** If $a > 1$ then $a^m < a^n$ whenever $m < n$ in $\mathbb{N}$; if $a = 1$ then $a^n = 1$ for all $n$; and if $0 < a < 1$ then $a^m > a^n$ whenever $m < n$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ then $a^{-1} > 0$.
2. If $0 < a < b$ then $0 < b^{-1} < a^{-1}$.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathbb{R}$ is the ambient ordered field
([[def-ordered-field]], [[def-field]]).

**Natural exponents.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to
the set $\mathbb{R}$, the starting element $1$ and the function

$$a^{-n} := (a^n)^{-1}.$$

invertible, that is, that $a^n \ne 0$. This is a proof obligation and not an

`deps` (SCHEMA §3). Given $a^n \ne 0$, the value $(a^n)^{-1}$ is a single
well-determined element, because multiplicative inverses in a field are unique
([[lem-of-inverse-unique]]).

**Integer exponents.** Every integer $m$ ([[def-integers]]) is either

embedding $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]],

injective. The two clauses above therefore define $a^m$ for every
$m \in \mathbb{Z}$ whenever $a \ne 0$, and for every $m \in \mathbb{N}$ for
arbitrary $a$. The two exponent domains are disjoint: the natural clause
handles $m \ge 0$, including $m = 0$, while the negative clause requires
$n \ge 1$ and therefore handles only $m < 0$.

for every $x \in F$ there is a natural number $n \ge 1$ with $x < n \cdot 1_F$,
where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of the ordered field $F$
([[def-ordered-field]]). Equivalently, the canonical naturals are cofinal in $F$.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathbb{R}$ is the ambient ordered field

In any ordered field $F$ with positive cone $P$, the multiplicative identity
satisfies $0 < 1$; that is, $1 \in P$.

derivations.claim: Set $b_r=r^{d-1}16^{-r}$. By [F11] and [F13], for $r\ge1$ and $j\ge1$ we have $r^{-j}\le r^{-1}$; hence $b_{r+1}/b_r=(1+1/r)^{d-1}/16\le(1+(2^{d-1}-1)/r)/16$. Put $C:=2^{d-1}-1\ge0$. If $C=0$, take $R=1$; if $C>0$, [F14] gives a natural $R\ge1$ with $2C<R$. For every $r\ge R$, the ratio is at most $(3/2)/16=3/32<1/2$. Induction then bounds the tail by a geometric sequence with ratio $1/2$, so [F7] bounds its partial sums; adding the finite initial segment bounds every partial sum. The partial sums form a nonempty bounded set, so [F12] defines a finite supremum $T_d$.

A node of $X_\ell=\{k/2^{\ell+1}:0\le k\le2^{\ell+1}\}$ belongs to every level at least its minimal level $t(x)$. The three nodes of minimal level zero are $0,1/2,1$. For $r\ge1$, a node of minimal level $r$ has reduced form $p/2^{r+1}$ with odd $p$ and $0<p<2^{r+1}$, giving exactly $2^r$ choices. A node tuple belongs to $\mathcal N_{\Lambda_n}$ iff its minimal-level vector $t$ satisfies $|t|_1\le n$: that condition itself supplies an admissible index, and any index containing the tuple has each coordinate at least its minimal level. Multiplying the coordinate counts and summing over these vectors proves the exact work formula.

Fix a finite $F\subseteq\mathbb N_0^d\setminus\Lambda_n$ and group its indices by the nonempty active-coordinate subset $S$ of size $k$. If the positive coordinates sum to $m=n+r$, then $r\ge1$; there are at most $\binom{m-1}{k-1}$ such tuples by [F6]. Since this coefficient counts $(k-1)$-element subsets, listing each subset in increasing order injects them into ordered $(k-1)$-tuples with entries from a set of $m$ elements; thus $\binom{m-1}{k-1}\le m^{k-1}$. Since $m=n+r\le(n+1)r$, each fixed-$S$ contribution is at most $M_S(17/2880)^k16^{-n}(n+1)^{d-1}r^{d-1}16^{-r}$. Summing over the finitely many $r$ present in $F$, enlarging to the partial sum through the largest such $r$, and then summing over $S$ gives $\sum_{\ell\in F}|\delta_\ell(f)|\le T_d\|f\|_{\mathrm{mix},d}16^{-n}(n+1)^{d-1}$. Taking the supremum over finite $F$ bounds the omitted absolute-detail tail; [F4] gives the first error inequality.

By the node classification and exact formula in step 1.2, the number of level vectors with $|t|_1=m$ is $\binom{m+d-1}{d-1}$ by [F5], and each has $\prod_j a_{t_j}\le3^d2^m$. Since $\binom{m+d-1}{d-1}$ counts $(d-1)$-element subsets, increasing enumeration injects them into ordered $(d-1)$-tuples from a set of $m+d$ elements, giving $\binom{m+d-1}{d-1}\le(m+d)^{d-1}$. The finite geometric sum is $\sum_{m=0}^n2^m=\sum_{m=0}^n(2^{m+1}-2^m)=2^{n+1}-1<2^{n+1}$: the term identity follows from [F15], telescoping from [F9], and $1>0$ from [F16]. Hence $W_{n,d}\le3^d(n+d)^{d-1}\sum_{m=0}^n2^m<2\cdot3^d2^n(n+d)^{d-1}\le D_d2^n(n+1)^{d-1}$, since $n+d\le d(n+1)$. For a lower bound, restrict to vectors with all $t_j\ge1$ and $|t|_1=n$. There are $\binom{n-1}{d-1}$ by [F6], and each contributes $\prod_ja_{t_j}=2^n$.

From step 2.2, $2^n\ge W_{n,d}/(D_d(n+1)^{d-1})$, so $16^{-n}\le D_d^4W_{n,d}^{-4}(n+1)^{4(d-1)}$. The exact work formula in step 1.2 contains the contribution of the vector $t=(n-d+1,1,\ldots,1)$, whose entries are positive because $n\ge2d$; this contribution is $2^n$, so $W_{n,d}\ge2^n$. Hence [F8] yields $\log(2+W_{n,d})\ge n\log2$. As $n\ge2d\ge2$, $n+1\le(3/2)n\le3\log(2+W_{n,d})/\log2$. Substituting these inequalities into step 2.1's error estimate gives the second bound with the stated $C_d$.

Use the dyadic composite-Simpson hierarchy of
[[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]]. Let $d\ge1$. For
$S=\{j_1<\cdots<j_k\}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$, define
$$D_Sf:=\partial_{x_{j_k}}^4\cdots\partial_{x_{j_1}}^4f,$$
so these derivatives are applied in increasing coordinate order; set
$D_\varnothing f=f$. Assume every $D_Sf$ is continuous on the closed cube,
with the one-sided endpoint convention of
[[def-higher-derivatives-and-smoothness]], and choose finite bounds $M_S\ge0$
such that $|D_Sf(x)|\le M_S$ on $[0,1]^d$. For
$\ell\in\mathbb N_0^d$, put $S(\ell):=\{j:\ell_j\ge1\}$ and
$$\delta_\ell(f):=(\Delta_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes\Delta_{\ell_d}^{(d)})(f).$$
Then
$$|\delta_\ell(f)|\le M_{S(\ell)}\left(\frac{17}{2880}\right)^{|S(\ell)|}16^{-\sum_{j\in S(\ell)}\ell_j}.$$
Moreover, for every finite $F\subseteq\mathbb N_0^d$,
$$\sum_{\ell\in F}|\delta_\ell(f)|\le\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}}M_S\left(\frac{17}{43200}\right)^{|S|}<\infty.$$

Use the dyadic composite-Simpson hierarchy of
[[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]]. Let $d\ge1$, $n\ge2d$, and let
$f:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R$ satisfy the
continuous mixed fourth-derivative hypotheses and bounds $M_S$ of
[[lem-smolyak-mixed-simpson-detail-decay]]. Define the isotropic index set
$$\Lambda_n:=\{\ell\in\mathbb N_0^d:|\ell|_1\le n\},$$
and let $W_{n,d}:=|\mathcal N_{\Lambda_n}|$ be the distinct-node work count
of [[def-smolyak-cubature]] and [[alg-smolyak-node-deduplication]]. For a

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

derivations.claim: Fix an interior $y\in(0,1)$ and write $g(h)=f(y+h,y)=|h|^3$ for sufficiently small positive and negative $h$. By [F4]–[F5], on the two sides $g'(h)=3h|h|$ and $g''(h)=6|h|$ for $h\ne0$. The difference quotients at zero give $g'(0)=0$ and $g''(0)=\lim_{h\to0}3|h|=0$. The derivative of $g''$ at zero would require $\lim_{h\to0}(g''(h)-g''(0))/h=\lim_{h\to0}6|h|/h$, whose right-hand value is $6$ and left-hand value is $-6$. Thus $g'''(0)$ does not exist, so $g^{(4)}(0)$ cannot exist. By [F3], the required derivative therefore fails at the interior diagonal point $(y,y)$.

Since [F1] requires $D_{\{1\}}f=\partial_x^4f$ to exist continuously everywhere, the failure in step 1.1 violates a stated hypothesis of the rate theorem [F2]. The theorem makes no such rate claim for this ridge.

For every fixed $y$, the same formulas give $\partial_x^2f(x,y)=6|x-y|$, including its value zero on the diagonal; the same one-sided calculations apply at $x=0,1$. By symmetry $\partial_y^2f(x,y)=6|x-y|$ as well. These partials are continuous and bounded by $6$ on the square since $|x-y|\le1$, illustrating that lower-order smoothness does not imply the fourth-order condition used here.

citations.quote:
Fix a dimension $d\ge1$. A finite set $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb N_0^d$ is
**downward closed** if, whenever $\ell\in\Lambda$ and $\ell_j>0$, the index
$\ell-e_j$ also belongs to $\Lambda$; here $e_j$ is the $j$th coordinate unit
vector. In this pair an admissible Smolyak set is a nonempty finite downward-
closed $\Lambda$ that contains $0$.

For a level hierarchy from [[def-smolyak-univariate-level-hierarchy]], define
the **Smolyak cubature functional**
$$Q_\Lambda(f):=\sum_{\ell\in\Lambda}(\Delta_{\ell_1}^{(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes\Delta_{\ell_d}^{(d)})(f).$$
Each summand is a finite signed weighted sum. Expanding all differences and
adding coefficients at equal points gives one finite signed weight for each
distinct node in
$$\mathcal N_\Lambda:=\bigcup_{\ell\in\Lambda}X_{\ell_1}\times\cdots\times X_{\ell_d}.$$
The **node-union work count** for this direct evaluation convention is
$W(\Lambda):=|\mathcal N_\Lambda|$, so shared nodes are counted once. A
combined weight may be negative or zero; no positivity claim follows from the
definition.

**Input:** dimension $d\ge1$, a finite downward-closed $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb
N_0^d$ containing $0$, the finitely many levels required by $\Lambda$, a
function $f$ evaluable at their nodes, and for each exact node a canonical key
in a totally ordered set. Keys must agree exactly if and only if the real node
tuples agree. If any required rule or key is missing, return `invalid-input`.

**Output:** the sorted list of distinct node tuples with their combined signed
weights, the value $Q_\Lambda(f)$, and the actual evaluation count
$W(\Lambda)$.

1. Expand each detail $\Delta_\ell$ in the finite Smolyak sum of
   [[def-smolyak-cubature]] by replacing each coordinate factor
   $\Delta_0$ with $Q_0$ and each $\Delta_r$ ($r\ge1$) with
   $Q_r-Q_{r-1}$. Enumerate the resulting finite signed tensor rules in
   lexicographic multi-index order.
2. For each tensor rule, enumerate its finite node tuples in lexicographic
   coordinate-key order. Add its signed coefficient to a finite map indexed by
   the exact tuple key; initialize an unseen key with coefficient $0$.
3. Form $\mathcal N_\Lambda=\bigcup_{\ell\in\Lambda}
   X_{\ell_1}\times\cdots\times X_{\ell_d}$, sort its distinct exact keys, and
   evaluate $f$ once at each of these keys. Return the map of combined
   coefficients and the finite sum of coefficient times function value. Set
   $W(\Lambda):=|\mathcal N_\Lambda|$, including any node whose combined
   coefficient is zero; this is the work convention used in this pair.

This is an exact-real finite procedure. Approximate floating-point node
comparisons, arithmetic, and function-evaluation error are outside its claims.

Let $a<b$, $m=(a+b)/2$, $d=(b-a)/2$, and $f\in C[a,b]$. For $n\ge1$, set $g(t):=f(m+dt)$ on $[-1,1]$, let $y_j=g(\cos(j\pi/n))$, and form $a_0,\ldots,a_n$ from the DCT-I coefficients in [[thm-na-clenshaw-curtis-interpolation-coefficients]]. With the Chebyshev moments $\mu_k$ of [[lem-na-chebyshev-integral-moments]], define
$$Q_{n,[a,b]}(f):=d\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_k\mu_k.$$
For $n=0$, define instead
$$Q_{0,[a,b]}(f):=(b-a)f(m),$$
the midpoint rule. This is the explicit endpoint and zero-degree convention for Clenshaw–Curtis quadrature. The sums and coefficients are exact real quantities; finite-precision evaluation is a separate algorithm.

Let $a<b$, $n\ge0$, and $f\in C[a,b]$. Put $m=(a+b)/2$, $d=(b-a)/2$, and $g(t)=f(m+dt)$ on $[-1,1]$. Let $E_n(g)$ and $\Lambda_n^L$ be the best uniform polynomial error and the Chebyshev–Lobatto interpolation norm from [[def-best-uniform-polynomial-approximation-error-and-chebyshev-interpolants]]. The rule $Q_{n,[a,b]}$ of [[def-na-clenshaw-curtis-quadrature]] is exact for every polynomial of degree at most $n$, and
$$\left|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-Q_{n,[a,b]}(f)\right|\le(b-a)(1+\Lambda_n^L)E_n(g).$$
Because affine pullback preserves the supremum norm and polynomial degree, $E_n(g)$ is also the best degree-$n$ uniform error of $f$ on $[a,b]$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles. If $a:A\to\mathbb R$ and $b:B\to\mathbb R$ are continuous and $f(x,y):=a(x)b(y)$, then
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\left(\int_Aa\right)\left(\int_Bb\right).$$
In particular, if $f(x,y)=a(x)$ is independent of $y$, then $\int_{A\times B}f=\operatorname{vol}(B)\int_Aa$.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

derivations.claim: The Given rules are the $n=1$ and $n=2$ rules. By [F3], their normalized nodes are $(1+\cos(j\pi/n))/2$; [F5] and [F8] give $X_0=\{0,1\}$ and $X_1=\{0,1/2,1\}$. By [F4], these rules are exact through degrees $1$ and $2$, respectively. Writing the level-zero weights as $w_0,w_1$, exactness on $1$ and $x$ gives $w_0+w_1=1$ and $w_1=1/2$, hence $Q_0(x)=Q_0(x^2)=1/2$. Also $Q_1(x)=1/2$ and $Q_1(x^2)=1/3$ by exactness and [F6]. Thus $\Delta_1(x)=0$ and $\Delta_1(x^2)=-1/6$.

Since $f$ is a product, its tensor details factor into one-dimensional values. The zero-index term is $Q_0(x^2)Q_0(x)^3=1/16$. The $e_1$ term is $\Delta_1(x^2)Q_0(x)^3=-1/48$, and each $e_j$ term for $j=2,3,4$ vanishes because $\Delta_1(x)=0$. Therefore $Q_{\Lambda_1}(f)=1/16-1/48=1/24$. By [F6]–[F7], $I_4(f)=(1/3)(1/2)^3=1/24$, so the cubature is exact.

The node union is $X_0^4$ together with, for each coordinate $j$, the $8$ points whose $j$th coordinate is $1/2$ and whose other coordinates are endpoints. Those four midpoint sets are disjoint from one another and from the $16$ corners, so $W(\Lambda_1)=16+4\cdot8=48$. The full tensor level-one grid has $|X_1|^4=3^4=81$ nodes.
